themes.global: The frontier stopped being the story and price did. OpenAI cut Luna 80% three weeks after shipping it, Chinese open-weight models peaked at 46% of US enterprise tokens, and Meta put a 30B agent model on a single consumer GPU under Apache 2.0. Meanwhile capability quietly jumped anyway — Astra closed ten decades-old maths problems for $2,000 of compute — and Google lost Jeff Dean and three of its founding AI names in one afternoon.
themes.eu-policy: August 2 was the day the AI Act started to bite: high-risk duties slipped to 2027/2028, but Article 50 transparency — chatbot disclosure, AI-content marking, deepfake labelling — and the Commission's GPAI enforcement powers went live on schedule. That turned data residency from a slide into a procurement checkbox, which is exactly the door Mistral walked through. Closer to home, Copenhagen put DKK 110M and a Deputy Prorector behind AI, and Denmark held its first national AI-safety conference.

items.title: Astra closes ten open maths problems for $2,000
items.subtitle: Lean 4 certificates, zero unproven steps
items.summary: OpenAI introduced Astra — still unreleased — by publishing solutions to ten problems across high-dimensional geometry, coding theory, group theory, quantum complexity, lattice cryptography and extremal combinatorics, each open for a decade or more. One establishes the existence of non-sofic groups. The release is a 249-page manuscript collection with machine-checkable Lean 4 certificates and a 'sorry' count of zero, meaning no step was left unproven. Compute cost: roughly $2,000. Humans wrote the papers; OpenAI credits the model with the reasoning.
items.whyItMatters: Formal verification is what separates this from the usual benchmark claim — a Lean certificate either compiles or it doesn't, so there is no grading dispute. It is not a first of its kind: DeepMind's AlphaProof produced Lean-checked proofs in 2024 and AlphaEvolve found new results on open problems. What stands out here is the age of the problems and the cost — decades-open questions, closed end-to-end for about $2,000.
items.whyForUs: The transferable idea is the verifier, not the maths: pair a generative model with something that can mechanically check its output, and you can let it search much harder. That's a demo-sized pattern — try it with a type checker, a test suite, or a schema validator in the loop.

items.title: Jeff Dean leaves Google after 27 years
items.subtitle: Ghemawat, Vinyals and Le go with him
items.summary: Google's chief scientist — employee number 30 — told the company he was leaving on August 5. Sanjay Ghemawat, DeepMind research VP Oriol Vinyals and Google Brain founding member Quoc Le walked out with him to start Discovery Loop. Notably, Alphabet is itself a founding investor and cloud partner, so this is less a clean break than it looks; a round was reported as still in discussions with Radical Ventures and Khosla, with Lightspeed, Kleiner Perkins and Doerr Capital participating. The pitch: the scientific method is a loop — hypothesise, run, evaluate — and loops can be automated and run faster than any human team. Between them the four have their names on MapReduce, Bigtable, Spanner, TensorFlow, seq2seq and AlphaStar.
items.whyItMatters: This is not a normal executive departure. Much of the infrastructure the rest of the industry runs on was built by these four, and they left together for a thesis about automating research itself. That Alphabet funded them on the way out says it would rather hold a stake than lose the bet entirely.
items.whyForUs: Watch what Discovery Loop open-sources. Anything aimed at automating the experiment loop tends to show up as tooling the rest of us can use within a year — and 'automate my own iteration loop' is a good frame for a side project.

items.title: Meta ships a 30B agent model that runs on one GPU
items.subtitle: Muse Glimmer, Apache 2.0, open weights
items.summary: Muse Glimmer is a 30-billion-parameter open-weight multimodal model under Apache 2.0, built to run agentic tasks locally on a Mac or PC with a single consumer graphics card rather than in a data centre. Zuckerberg paired it with a 6,500-word essay, 'The Future is for Everyone', arguing for more open-weight releases and a federal role in safety testing, plus a $1B fund for communities near Meta data centres. Meta also said it will open the weights of Muse Spark 1.2, its most capable model.
items.whyItMatters: Apache 2.0 on a genuinely capable agent model is the permissive end of the spectrum — no usage ceiling, no acceptable-use rider. It puts real pressure on the assumption that agents have to be a hosted API call.
items.whyForUs: This is the most directly demo-able thing in the roundup. If you already have Ollama or LM Studio from session #7, Glimmer is the obvious next thing to pull down — a local agent with no per-token cost and no data leaving the laptop. Someone please bring this to a Show & Tell.

items.title: OpenAI cuts GPT-5.6 Luna by 80%
items.subtitle: Three weeks after launching it
items.summary: Luna dropped from $1.00 to $0.20 per million input tokens and $6.00 to $1.20 output for short contexts — an 80% cut made three weeks after the GPT-5.6 family shipped on July 9. Terra fell 20% ($2.50 → $2.00 in, $15 → $12 out). Sol was left unchanged at $5/$30. Reporting tied the move to cost sensitivity among enterprise buyers rather than to any new model.
items.whyItMatters: Cutting a flagship tier by 80% within a month of launch is not a promotion, it's a response to pricing pressure. The competitive axis has moved from capability to cost per token.
items.whyForUs: Re-run your cost estimates. Anything you shelved earlier this year as too expensive to call per-request is now plausibly five times cheaper — batch jobs, per-row enrichment, and eval loops especially.

items.title: Chinese models hit 46% of US enterprise tokens
items.subtitle: Up from 11% a year earlier
items.summary: A CNBC investigation using OpenRouter data put Chinese models at a weekly peak of 46% of tokens routed through the platform by mid-2026 — reporting framed this around US enterprise usage — against an 11% average over the prior twelve months and 4.5% in the first half of 2025. DeepSeek is the single largest vendor on the router at 17.6%, with Alibaba's Qwen on 13.9%. The driver is price — open Chinese models run roughly 60–90% cheaper than the leading US offerings — and stickiness, since teams that build around a model rarely migrate back.
items.whyItMatters: Adoption is following cost, not leaderboards, and it's happening inside US enterprises rather than around them. That reframes the 'which lab is ahead' conversation as largely irrelevant to what actually gets deployed.
items.whyForUs: Worth an honest look before defaulting to a US API. Also worth reading the licence and thinking about where inference physically runs — see the AI Act item below, because for EU deployments that is now a compliance question, not a preference.

items.title: Claude in Chrome goes generally available
items.subtitle: Autonomous browser actions on every paid plan
items.summary: Anthropic took its Chrome extension out of preview on August 26 for Pro, Max, Team and Enterprise — not the free tier. The headline change is that Claude can now act in the browser without approving every individual step (there is an opt-out), with a safety classifier validating each action and prompt-injection defences in place. It reads pages, clicks, types and fills forms across multi-step tasks. It is available in Claude Code; Cowork's own built-in browser is a related but separate, still-evolving surface.
items.whyItMatters: Browser agents have been demoed for two years and shipped cautiously, because a model that can click things on your behalf is a real security surface. Moving from per-action approval to classifier-gated autonomy is the bet that the defences are now good enough.
items.whyForUs: Concretely useful for the boring half of community admin — pulling RSVPs, filling forms, reconciling lists. Try it on something low-stakes first and watch what it actually clicks.

items.title: Google ships three Gemini models, none of them Pro
items.subtitle: Including one tuned for finding vulnerabilities
items.summary: Gemini 3.6 Flash, 3.5 Flash-Lite and 3.5 Flash Cyber landed on July 21 — no 3.5 Pro. Flash improves token efficiency and agentic planning at a lower price than 3.5 Flash; Flash-Lite is the cheapest in class; Flash Cyber is fine-tuned for finding and fixing security vulnerabilities, but is restricted to governments and trusted partners under a pilot rather than generally available. Product lead Logan Kilpatrick said 3.5 Pro is in partner testing and that the team has begun its most ambitious pre-training run yet, for Gemini 4.
items.whyItMatters: Three cheap, specialised models instead of one flagship is the same cost-pressure story from a different direction. A model fine-tuned for vulnerability discovery is also a notable first for a mainstream general-purpose family.
items.whyForUs: Flash-Lite is the practical takeaway — a sensible default for high-volume, low-stakes calls. Flash Cyber is the one to watch rather than use: you can't get it yet, but a mainstream family shipping a vulnerability-hunting variant tells you where the tooling is going.

items.title: OpenAI files confidentially for an IPO
items.subtitle: $852B valuation, timing still open
items.summary: OpenAI submitted a confidential draft S-1 to the SEC on May 22, with Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley leading (JPMorgan also reportedly involved), at an $852B valuation carried over from the round it closed on 31 March. It was not first in the queue: SpaceX had filed confidentially on 1 April, and Anthropic followed on 1 June at a reported $965B. By late June, Reuters reported OpenAI may wait until 2027; the company says it hasn't committed to a timeline because 'there are things we want to do that are likely easier as a private company,' and that the filing simply preserves the option. No public filing or final terms as of late August.
items.whyItMatters: A confidential draft is optionality, not a date — but it forces the financials into a form regulators and eventually the public can read, which is the first time anyone outside will see what frontier-model economics actually look like.
items.whyForUs: The interesting part for builders is the eventual disclosure: real inference margins, real compute costs. Until then, treat 'OpenAI is going public' headlines with the hedging the company itself is using.

items.title: The AI Act's transparency rules went live on August 2
items.subtitle: High-risk duties slipped to 2027 and 2028
items.summary: The Digital Omnibus pushed the high-risk regime — conformity assessment, registration, risk management, data governance, logging, human oversight — out to 2 December 2027 for Annex III systems and 2 August 2028 for product-embedded Annex I systems. Parliament approved the amendments on 16 June, the Council gave final approval on 29 June, and the text was published in the Official Journal on 24 July, entering into force on 27 July. What was not delayed: Article 50 transparency duties — chatbot disclosure, marking of AI-generated content, deepfake labelling — and the Commission's GPAI enforcement powers, all applicable from 2 August 2026. The single carve-out is machine-readable watermarking for systems already on the market, which has until 2 December 2026.
items.whyItMatters: The deferral got the headlines and the part that actually applies to most people did not. Article 50 covers anyone shipping a chatbot or generating synthetic media in the EU — a far larger group than the high-risk category everyone was worrying about.
items.whyForUs: If your side project has a chat interface or generates images, audio or video for EU users, disclosure and marking apply to you now — with two caveats worth knowing: Article 50(4) exempts evidently artistic, satirical or fictional work that is appropriately disclosed, and some duties land on whoever deploys the system rather than whoever built it. Good Lean Coffee topic — most of us are shipping exactly what Article 50 describes.

items.title: Mistral turns sovereignty into a product
items.subtitle: Regional endpoints GA, 1 GW by 2030
items.summary: Nine days after the AI Act's transparency rules landed, Mistral made Regional Endpoints generally available — customers pick whether inference runs in Europe or the US — added a Priority Tier with uptime SLAs, and started hosting third-party open models on the same infrastructure, beginning with Z.ai's GLM-5.2. It also launched a coalition selling 'European Compute Units' to fund up to 1 GW of European capacity by 2030, with Amadeus, ASML, Capgemini, Caisse des Dépôts and CMA CGM named. In July, Microsoft and Mistral expanded a multibillion-dollar deal to put NVIDIA Vera Rubin GPUs in European data centres.
items.whyItMatters: Data residency stopped being a talking point the day enforcement started. Selling compute commitments as a subscription is an unusual financing model — it makes enterprise buyers underwrite the infrastructure they say they want.
items.whyForUs: If you are building anything that touches personal data for an EU employer, 'where does inference run' is now a question you will be asked. Regional endpoints are a straightforward answer, and hosting an open Chinese model on European infrastructure is a neat sidestep of the tension in item 5.

items.title: Copenhagen University puts DKK 110M behind AI
items.subtitle: And appoints a Deputy Prorector for it
items.summary: UCPH announced a DKK 110 million initiative on 27 August, with Professor Morten Axel Pedersen becoming Deputy Prorector of AI from 1 September. The work splits into two missions: 'AI at UCPH', integrating AI across research, teaching and administration — explicitly including when it should *not* be used — and 'UCPH with AI', researching digital sovereignty, ethics and regulation, and building the competencies an AI-changed job market needs.
items.whyItMatters: A university creating a pro-rector-level AI post is an institutional signal, not a pilot project. Denmark's largest university is treating this as a decade-long structural change rather than a tooling question.
items.whyForUs: This is on our doorstep. UCPH will be hiring, funding and running events, and 'when should we *not* use AI' is a framing worth stealing for a session — it is a more interesting discussion than another tool demo.

items.title: Denmark holds its first AI safety conference
items.subtitle: Next one is 27 February 2027, free
items.summary: The inaugural Danish AI Safety Conference ran on Saturday 22 August in Brøndby, organised by Søren Elverlin — the first national conference in Denmark dedicated to catastrophic and existential risk from increasingly capable AI. Rasmus Herlo (UCPH) gave the keynote on AI systems and interventions, with Lukas Galke Poech (SDU) on mechanistic interpretability, Daniel Juhl on security engineering in AI control, and five lightning talks from attendees.
items.whyItMatters: A national safety conference existing at all marks the point where the topic moved from online discourse to a room with a venue and a programme. That it filled a Saturday in August says something about the appetite.
items.whyForUs: The next one is Saturday 27 February 2027, registration is free and capacity is limited. It also runs a lightning-talk slot for attendees — a low-stakes way for someone from this group to present outside our own room. Worth putting on the calendar now.
